meta.name: Boykin Spaniel
meta.tagline: The Boykin Spaniel is South Carolina's state dog: a compact, liver-brown spaniel bred to flush and retrieve turkey and waterfowl from small boats. It's friendly and easy to train, but it needs plenty of daily exercise, regular ear care, and a breeder who does the club's full health-test panel.
meta.excerpt: Boykin Spaniels are friendly, trainable, medium-sized hunting spaniels that get along well with kids and other dogs. They also need hours of activity as puppies, regular ear care, and parents tested for hips, eyes, EIC, CEA and DM.
meta.meta_description: Boykin Spaniel guide: South Carolina's state dog, AKC Sporting Group energy, EIC, CEA and DM testing, ear care, training, and what a well-bred pup costs.
meta.title_tag: Boykin Spaniel: Temperament, Care, Health, Cost
meta.quick_answer: The Boykin Spaniel is a medium sporting dog, weighing 25–40 lbs and living 10–15 years. Plan on 60–90 min of exercise a day. Grooming is moderate; training is easy. It is good with kids. First-time owners can manage one with research and commitment.

intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: What Is a Boykin Spaniel?
intro.html:
The Boykin Spaniel is a South Carolina original, and the AKC calls it "among the handful of AKC breeds wholly developed in the 20th century." The story starts in the early 1900s with a stray brown spaniel that befriended Spartanburg banker Alexander White. White named the dog Dumpy and sent him to his hunting partner, Whit Boykin, near Camden. Sources differ on the year: the AKC says around 1900, the South Carolina Encyclopedia around 1905. Boykin built a breeding program around Dumpy, and the AKC says the crosses included the Chesapeake Bay Retriever, Cocker Spaniel, English Springer Spaniel and American Water Spaniel.

The goal was a dog for hunting turkey and waterfowl in the swamps along the Wateree River: small and light enough to ride in the portable section boats of the day, and able to retrieve on land or water. The breed standard still calls it "the little brown dog that doesn't rock the boat."

The Boykin Spaniel Society was founded in Camden in 1977 and started its registry in 1979. South Carolina made the Boykin its official state dog in an act signed on March 26, 1985; Governor Richard Riley had proclaimed September 1, 1984, as Boykin Spaniel Day. The AKC granted full recognition in 2009, placing the breed in the Sporting Group; its AKC parent club is the Boykin Spaniel Club & Breeders Association of America (BSCBAA). This guide covers what the breed needs day to day, the club's health-test panel, and what a well-bred puppy costs.

appearance.label: Physical
appearance.heading: What does a Boykin Spaniel look like?
appearance.html:
A medium-sized, solidly built spaniel, slightly longer than tall. The AKC standard sets the ideal height at 15½–18 inches for males and 14–16½ inches for females, and a variance of more than an inch either way is a major fault. The AKC gives weights of 30–40 lbs for males and 25–35 lbs for females. The tail is docked to 3–5 inches.

The color is always solid liver: a deep reddish brown in shades from light to very dark chocolate. A small amount of white on the chest is the only white allowed, and sun bleaching is acceptable. Eyes range from yellow to amber to brown. The coat runs from flat to slightly wavy to curly, medium length, with light feathering on the ears, chest, legs and belly. It is usually a single coat but may have some undercoat, and the standard calls the breed "wash and wear." The toes are webbed and well padded.

temperament.label: Personality
temperament.heading: What is the temperament of a Boykin Spaniel?
temperament.html:
The standard describes the Boykin as "friendly, a willing worker, intelligent and easy to train," a dog that thrives on human companionship and gets along well with other dogs and children. The AKC calls it a tough, energetic hunting dog that is gentle and contented in the home, and the parent club says Boykins are very good with children, while adding that any dog should be supervised around young kids.

The catch is energy. The BSCBAA describes a physically active spaniel "designed for working all day in the field," and warns that a Boykin left alone for long periods "might find their own amusement." The Boykin Spaniel Society goes further: puppies need several hours of attention and exercise every day, and Boykin puppyhood can last three years or more.

Two other traits to know about. As a retrieving breed, Boykins may be mouthy, so plan on teaching them what they can carry. And the club calls them "responsible barkers": they'll alert you to a visitor or a strange noise, but they shouldn't bark without reason. They are friendly rather than protective, so don't expect a guard dog.

mikes_take.label: A Realistic Take
mikes_take.heading: What I'd Tell a Friend Thinking About a Boykin
mikes_take.html:
If you already spend your weekends outdoors, hiking, paddling, running or hunting, I think the Boykin is one of the best-sized sporting dogs you can get. You get real bird-dog drive in a 25–40 lb body that fits in a hatchback, a small boat or a smaller house, and a temperament that's easy with kids and other dogs.

What I'd warn a friend about: a small spaniel is not a lap dog. The breed's own society says puppyhood can last three years or more and that puppies need several hours of attention and exercise every day. If that sentence makes you tired, look at a lower-energy breed.

The other thing I'd be strict about is health testing. "Vet checked" or "hips done" is not enough. The parent club requires six tests of breeding dogs: an eye exam, patellas, hips, and DNA tests for exercise-induced collapse (EIC), Collie eye anomaly (CEA) and degenerative myelopathy (DM). Hip results can't be finalized before 24 months, so the Boykin Spaniel Society tells buyers to check that both parents are at least 2 years old. A litter from a one-year-old parent is a red flag.

And make ear care a weekly habit. The AKC notes that Boykins can develop ear problems if they're neglected, especially after swimming. That is much easier to prevent than to treat.

care.label: Daily Life
care.heading: How much exercise and grooming does a Boykin Spaniel need?
care.html:
Exercise

The AKC describes Boykins as moderate- to high-energy dogs that need lots of exercise every day and do best with active people who hike, run or bike. Plan on 60–90 minutes of real activity for most adults, split across the day: long walks, retrieving games and swimming where it's safe, plus short training sessions. Obedience, tracking, agility, rally and field events are all good outlets. If a Boykin ever wobbles, loses coordination or collapses during hard exercise, stop immediately and call your vet; that is one reason the EIC DNA test matters.

Grooming

  • Brushing: Weekly, and more often during heavier shedding; the parent club calls Boykins moderate shedders
  • Trimming: The standard allows tidying the head, throat, ears, tail and feet, but the coat should never be shaved
  • Ears: Check and clean regularly, especially after swimming, working in water or bathing; ask your vet or breeder which cleaner to use (AKC)
  • Nails and teeth: Trim nails regularly and brush teeth often (AKC)
  • Bathing: Occasional baths are enough for most dogs

Training

The AKC says Boykins are intelligent, eager to please and generally easy to train, and it recommends early socialization and puppy classes. They respond best to reward-based training. Useful early priorities are a reliable recall, a solid "give" or "drop it" for a mouthy retriever, calm crate or settle time for the long puppy phase, and loose-leash walking. If you plan to hunt, look for a trainer or club with retriever or spaniel field experience.

health.label: Wellness
health.heading: What health problems are common in the Boykin Spaniel?
health.html:
The AKC calls Boykins generally healthy, but the parent club lists the breed's most common problems as hip dysplasia, juvenile cataracts, patellar luxation, Collie eye anomaly and exercise-induced collapse. Through the CHIC program, the BSCBAA requires six tests of breeding dogs: an eye exam by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist, a patella evaluation, OFA or PennHIP hips, and DNA tests for EIC, CEA and DM. Cardiac and elbow evaluations are optional. The club also lists supplemental DNA tests, including one for a Boykin-type myotubular myopathy, and also lists testing for IVDD risk (CDDY).

ConditionWhat It Means
Hip DysplasiaListed first among the breed's common problems by the parent club. Both parents should have OFA or PennHIP hip results. Final OFA hip clearances can't be obtained before 24 months of age, which is why parents should be at least 2 years old.
Exercise-Induced Collapse (EIC)An inherited condition caused by a DNM1 gene mutation. Affected dogs can show muscle weakness, loss of coordination and a potentially life-threatening collapse after intense exercise (Patterson et al., 2008). A University of Minnesota-led study found carriers and affected dogs that had collapsed among Boykin Spaniels, and noted that not every dog with two copies will collapse (Minor et al., 2011). DNA test required since November 2015.
Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA)An inherited disorder of eye development. Effects range from no visual impairment to blindness in severe cases with retinal detachment, and the Boykin is one of the breeds in which it occurs (OMIA). It is recessive, so two carriers can produce affected puppies. DNA test required since November 2015.
Degenerative Myelopathy (DM)A progressive spinal cord disease that usually starts around 8 years or older with weakness in one hind leg, then both. Cornell's Riney Canine Health Center notes there is no cure, although physical therapy may slow it. Dogs with two copies of the variant are at higher risk but won't necessarily develop the disease. DNA test required since February 2018.
Juvenile Cataracts and Other Eye DiseaseThe parent club names juvenile cataracts among the breed's most common problems. Breeding dogs need an eye exam by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist, and the Boykin Spaniel Society sets no minimum age for it.
Patellar LuxationThe kneecap slips out of its groove, which can cause a skipping gait (American College of Veterinary Surgeons). An OFA patella evaluation is required; the Boykin Spaniel Society lists 12 months as the minimum age.
Heart (Pulmonic Stenosis)The Boykin Spaniel Society includes pulmonic stenosis in its list of seven inherited diseases and screens from 12 months. The BSCBAA lists a cardiac evaluation as optional, so ask whether the parents had one.
X-Linked Myotubular Myopathy (Boykin type)A fatal inherited muscle disease described in Boykins by NC State researchers. In that report, an affected male puppy showed progressive weakness by 3 months and was euthanized at 5 months, and three affected males from a later litter died by 2 weeks of age; the carrier dam and carrier females were clinically normal (Olby et al., 2020). The club lists a DNA test as a supplemental option; ask whether the dam has been tested.
Ears and SkinThe AKC notes ear problems if ears are neglected, especially after water work. The Boykin Spaniel Society says skin conditions are fairly common in some bloodlines, which is a good reason to ask about the parents' skin history.

Ask breeders for (both parents): All six BSCBAA-required results: eye exam, patellas, hips (OFA or PennHIP, 24 months or older), and EIC, CEA and DM DNA tests, recorded with OFA. Also ask about cardiac and elbow exams and the dam's MTM1 status. You can look up results by each dog's registered name on the OFA website.

cost.label: Budget
cost.heading: How much does a Boykin Spaniel cost?
cost.html:
The Boykin Spaniel Society gives buyers a price floor: "Prepare to spend $1000 and up or more for a well bred puppy." It also warns that most responsible breeders have waiting lists of a few months to several years. The other figures below are estimated ranges from Rover's 2026 cost-of-dog-ownership data, which covers all breeds and sizes, so a medium-sized Boykin will usually fall somewhere in the middle of each range.

Supplies and gear (crate, bed, leash, grooming tools)$260–$1,125$75–$175

Rover all-breed totals$1,145–$4,150 up-front (before the puppy price or any adoption fee), plus $1,460–$6,745 for the puppy year$1,930–$5,305

For a medium-sized dog, Rover puts typical care at $145–$505 a month and lifetime costs at $35,415–$43,285. For insurance context, the North American Pet Health Insurance Association reports that the average U.S. accident-and-illness premium for a dog was $836 in 2025; your quote will depend on age, location and plan. Budget for ear care and the occasional ear-infection visit, and for field training if you plan to hunt.

right_for_you.heading: Is a Boykin Spaniel Right for You?
good_fit: Active households — hikers, runners, paddlers or hunters — with time for exercise every day
Families with kids and other dogs; the standard describes a dog that gets along well with both
You want sporting-dog drive in a 25–40 lb dog that fits in a car or small boat
You enjoy training and want a people-focused, eager-to-please dog
You're willing to wait for a breeder who does the full health-test panel
not_fit: You want a calm, low-energy companion — Boykin puppyhood can last three years or more
The dog would be alone most of the day — bored Boykins find their own amusement
You won't keep up with regular ear checks, especially if the dog swims
You need a low-shedding or hypoallergenic dog — Boykins are moderate shedders
You want a puppy right away — good breeders often have waiting lists of months to years

finding.label: Next Steps
finding.heading: Where can you find a Boykin Spaniel puppy or rescue?
finding.html:
Buying from a Breeder

There are two good starting points. The BSCBAA breeder directory comes with the club's advice to "only seek breeders that do the required OFA testing," and the club says it does not endorse any listed breeder. The Boykin Spaniel Society's Gold & Silver Breeder Program lists breeders who have 100% of their breeding dogs veterinary-examined for the seven inherited diseases the society tracks; the society also says the list is not a recommendation or endorsement. Either way, check the results yourself: both parents at least 2 years old, OFA or PennHIP hips, an eye exam, patellas, and EIC, CEA and DM DNA results.

Two registries, one breed. Boykins may be registered with the AKC or with the Boykin Spaniel Society. The society says its papers can only be issued when the owners of the sire and dam are members, so ask up front which papers come with the puppy. Our guides to finding a responsible breeder and spotting puppy scams cover the rest of the checks, including deposits and contracts.

Rescue

Boykin Spaniel Rescue, Inc., the rescue listed on the AKC breed page, is dedicated to rescuing, rehoming and rehabilitating at-risk purebred Boykins and says it has more than 300 volunteers. Adoption starts with a $25 application; the adoption fee (as of February 2024) is $425 for puppies up to a year, $400 for dogs 1–6 and $375 for dogs 7 and older, and the rescue doesn't transport dogs, so you may need to travel to the foster home. Adult rescues can be a good fit if you'd rather skip the long puppy phase. If you're still deciding, see adopt or buy a dog.

faq.q: How much does a Boykin Spaniel puppy cost?
faq.a: The Boykin Spaniel Society tells buyers to "prepare to spend $1000 and up or more for a well bred puppy," and warns that most responsible breeders have waiting lists of a few months to several years. A price well below that, or a puppy available immediately with no health results for the parents, is a reason to slow down and check for a scam.

Yes. The parent club calls them moderate shedders and says frequent brushing keeps it under control. They are not hypoallergenic. Grooming is otherwise simple: weekly brushing, occasional baths, light trimming around the feet and ears, and regular ear cleaning.

faq.q: Are Boykin Spaniels good family dogs?
faq.a: For active families, yes. The breed standard describes a dog that gets along well with other dogs and children, and the parent club says Boykins are very good with kids, with the usual rule that young children and dogs should be supervised. The main challenge is energy: puppies need several hours of attention and exercise a day, and puppyhood can last three years or more.

faq.q: What is exercise-induced collapse (EIC) in Boykins?
faq.a: EIC is an inherited condition caused by a DNM1 gene mutation. Affected dogs can become weak, uncoordinated and collapse after intense exercise, and it can be life-threatening. Researchers have found the mutation in Boykin Spaniels, and the parent club has required an EIC DNA test of breeding dogs since 2015. If your dog ever wobbles or collapses during exercise, stop immediately and contact your vet.

faq.q: Why is the Boykin Spaniel South Carolina's state dog?
faq.a: The breed was developed in South Carolina for local hunters, and the 1985 law that made it the official state dog says it is the only dog originally bred for South Carolina hunters by South Carolinians. Governor Richard Riley signed the act on March 26, 1985, after proclaiming September 1, 1984, as Boykin Spaniel Day.

faq.q: What's the difference between AKC and Boykin Spaniel Society Boykins?
faq.a: They are the same breed with two registries. The Boykin Spaniel Society has kept a registry since 1979, and the AKC fully recognized the breed in 2009 with the BSCBAA as its parent club. Ask the breeder which papers the puppy comes with, and judge the breeder by health testing rather than by registry.
